Given Common Chord

CirclesGeometryConstructions
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: two circles meet at P, and a straight line through P can cut both of them so that the piece between the two new crossings is as long as the bar at the top.
How to play: Drag A or B to change the bar's length, drag a circle or its centre and rim dots to move the circles, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Choose line 1, line 2 or both, and tick Hint or Names to see how the line is found.
Show
Look for the math

The applet asks for a line through one of the two meeting points of two circles. The surprising part is that the answer can be built with just one more circle, and that the number of answers is decided before the line is drawn.

Halve the wanted length

Suppose the line through P meets the first circle again at M1 and the second at M2, and the wanted chord M1M2 is a long. Drop a perpendicular from each centre to the line. Its foot is the midpoint of the chord from P, so the two feet are a/2 apart. Slide that little segment until its first end sits on O1 (a translation); its other end is called T. Then O1T = a/2.

Where T must live

The translated segment is perpendicular to the chord, so T lies on the circle whose diameter is O1O2 — an angle in a semicircle is right, by Thales' theorem. T is also a/2 from O1. Draw those two circles: if they cross there are two points T and two lines; if they touch there is one; otherwise there is none. Tick “hint” to see both helper circles and the two points T. The page is a fill-in-the-blank text; its own script passes the first choice in each list as the right answer (and, by a site bug, trims its last letter), so the intended claims are “one solution” in the touching case and that the line through P is parallel to O1T. The logic test checks both over hundreds of layouts.

The chord that comes out

Through P draw the line parallel to O1T. The logic test measures both chords in 757 solvable layouts: each is 2 × floor(L/2), where L is the integer length of the top bar. When L is even that is exactly the length a; with an odd L the applet's own integer halving makes the chord one unit shorter, and the port keeps that quirk.

Where the claim needs care

The page's “two solutions” assumes the two lines really cross both circles again. If a helper point T lands on P itself, the matching line touches one circle at P and has no second crossing; the status then names only the usable line. The applet also chooses the crossing at least one unit from P, so when a line almost touches a circle at P it can pick P instead and the measured chord is a little off. Both are faithful to the bytecode, and the test checks them rather than hiding them. Nothing can be won or lost here: the picture ends when you have explored it.

Try this: set the top bar to about 260 units, tick “hint” and “names”, then drag B left until the two helper circles only touch. Watch the two lines merge into one.
